claim: Long INterspersed Element-1 (LINE-1 or L1) derived sequences comprise roughly 17% of human genomic DNA.
source: Long INterspersed Element-1 (LINE-1 or L1) derived sequences comprise roughly 17% of human genomic DNA (Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lander et al., 2001.

claim: The vast majority of L1 sequences are 5′ truncated, internally rearranged, or are inactivated by mutations and are unable to mobilize (i.e., retrotranspose) to new genomic locations.
source: The vast majority of L1 sequences are 5′ truncated, internally rearranged, or are inactivated by mutations and are unable to mobilize (i.e., retrotranspose) to new genomic locations (Grimaldi et al., 1984; Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grimaldi et al., 1984 and Lander et al., 2001.

claim: The average human genome contains 80–100 retrotransposition-competent (i.e., active) L1s.
source: However, it is estimated that the average human genome contains 80–100 retrotransposition-competent (i.e., active) L1s (Sassaman et al., 1997; Brouha et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sassaman et al., 1997 and Brouha et al., 2003.

claim: Active human L1s are approximately 6 kb in length.
source: Active human L1s are approximately 6 kb in length and contain a 5′ untranslated region (UTR), two open reading frames (ORF1 and ORF2), and a 3′ UTR that terminates in a poly (A) tail (Scott et al., 1987; Dombroski et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 1987 and Dombroski et al., 1991.

claim: Active human L1s contain a 5′ untranslated region (UTR), two open reading frames (ORF1 and ORF2), and a 3′ UTR that terminates in a poly (A) tail.
source: Active human L1s are approximately 6 kb in length and contain a 5′ untranslated region (UTR), two open reading frames (ORF1 and ORF2), and a 3′ UTR that terminates in a poly (A) tail (Scott et al., 1987; Dombroski et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 1987 and Dombroski et al., 1991.

claim: ORF1 encodes an ∼40 kDa protein (ORF1p) that binds L1 RNA as a trimer.
source: ORF1 encodes an ∼40 kDa protein (ORF1p) that binds L1 RNA as a trimer (Holmes et al., 1992; Hohjoh and Singer, 1996; Martin et al., 2003; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 1992; Hohjoh and Singer, 1996; Martin et al., 2003; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2009.

claim: ORF1p has nucleic acid chaperone activity.
source: ORF1p also has nucleic acid chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin and Bushman, 2001 and Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2009.

claim: ORF2 encodes an ∼150 kDa protein (ORF2p).
source: ORF2 encodes an ∼150 kDa protein (ORF2p) (Ergun et al., 2004; Doucet et al., 2010; Taylor et al., 2013b) with DNA endonuclease (Feng et al., 1996) and reverse transcriptase (Mathias et al., 1991) activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ergun et al., 2004; Doucet et al., 2010; Taylor et al., 2013b.

claim: ORF2p has DNA endonuclease activity.
source: ORF2 encodes an ∼150 kDa protein (ORF2p) (Ergun et al., 2004; Doucet et al., 2010; Taylor et al., 2013b) with DNA endonuclease (Feng et al., 1996) and reverse transcriptase (Mathias et al., 1991) activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feng et al., 1996.

claim: ORF2p has reverse transcriptase activity.
source: ORF2 encodes an ∼150 kDa protein (ORF2p) (Ergun et al., 2004; Doucet et al., 2010; Taylor et al., 2013b) with DNA endonuclease (Feng et al., 1996) and reverse transcriptase (Mathias et al., 1991) activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mathias et al., 1991.

claim: Both ORF1p and ORF2p are required for efficient L1 retrotransposition.
source: The development of a cultured cell assay definitively demonstrated that both ORF1p and ORF2p are required for efficient L1 retrotransposition (Moran et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moran et al., 1996.

claim: L1 retrotransposition occurs by a mechanism termed target-site primed reverse transcription (TPRT).
source: Subsequent biochemical studies revealed that L1 retrotransposition occurs by a mechanism termed target-site primed reverse transcription (TPRT) (Luan et al., 1993; Feng et al., 1996; Cost et al., 2002; Kulpa and Moran, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luan et al., 1993; Feng et al., 1996; Cost et al., 2002; Kulpa and Moran, 2006.

claim: Ongoing L1 retrotransposition events contribute to intra- and inter-individual genetic variation.
source: Ongoing L1 retrotransposition events contribute to intra- and inter-individual genetic variation and, on occasion, can disrupt gene function, leading to sporadic genetic diseases (Beck et al., 2011; Hancks and Kazazian, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beck et al., 2011 and Hancks and Kazazian, 2012.

claim: L1 retrotransposition can disrupt gene function, leading to sporadic genetic diseases.
source: Ongoing L1 retrotransposition events contribute to intra- and inter-individual genetic variation and, on occasion, can disrupt gene function, leading to sporadic genetic diseases (Beck et al., 2011; Hancks and Kazazian, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beck et al., 2011 and Hancks and Kazazian, 2012.

claim: Host cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to restrict L1 retrotransposition.
source: Given the mutagenic potential of active L1s, it is not surprising that host cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to restrict L1 retrotransposition (Levin and Moran, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levin and Moran, 2011.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type APOBEC3A cytidine deaminase protein (A3A) can potently inhibit L1 retrotransposition in cultured human cells.
source: Previous studies revealed that over-expression of the wild-type (WT) APOBEC3A cytidine deaminase protein (A3A), but not deaminase-defective A3A mutants, could potently inhibit L1 retrotransposition in cultured human cells (Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007; Niewiadomska et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007; Niewiadomska et al., 2007.

claim: Deaminase-defective A3A mutants do not potently inhibit L1 retrotransposition in cultured human cells.
source: Previous studies revealed that over-expression of the wild-type (WT) APOBEC3A cytidine deaminase protein (A3A), but not deaminase-defective A3A mutants, could potently inhibit L1 retrotransposition in cultured human cells (Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007; Niewiadomska et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007; Niewiadomska et al., 2007.

claim: Deamination events were not detected in L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of WT A3A in previous studies.
source: However, deamination events were not detected in L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of WT A3A (Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Kinomoto et al., 2007.

claim: A3A can inhibit L1 retrotransposition by deaminating transiently exposed single-strand DNA that arises during the process of L1 integration.
source: Here, we have used in vitro and in vivo assays to demonstrate that A3A can inhibit L1 retrotransposition by deaminating transiently exposed single-strand DNA that arises during the process of L1 integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro and in vivo assays described in the manuscript.

claim: In LEAP reactions that include RNase H, single-strand L1 cDNAs are rendered susceptible to A3A-mediated deamination.
source: In LEAP reactions that include RNase H, an enzyme that specifically degrades the RNA strand of an RNA/DNA heteroduplex, we report that single-strand L1 cDNAs are rendered susceptible to A3A-mediated deamination.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LEAP assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Newly synthesized L1 cDNAs remain annealed to their mRNA templates after reverse transcription, protecting the L1 cDNA from deamination by A3A.
source: These data suggest that newly synthesized L1 cDNAs remain annealed to their mRNA templates after reverse transcription, protecting the L1 cDNA from deamination by A3A.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing differential deamination patterns with and without RNase H.

claim: Engineered L1 retrotransposition events derived from cultured human cells that co-express A3A and the uracil DNA glycosylase inhibitor protein (UGI) contain strand-specific, A3A-mediated C-to-U deamination events.
source: We further demonstrate that engineered L1 retrotransposition events derived from cultured human cells that co-express A3A and the uracil DNA glycosylase inhibitor protein (UGI) contain strand-specific, A3A-mediated C-to-U deamination events.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cultured cell assays with UGI co-expression.

claim: A3A can deaminate single-strand genomic DNA in human cells.
source: Moreover, our results provide direct evidence that A3A can deaminate single-strand genomic DNA in human cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing deamination in flanking genomic DNA sequences.

claim: A3A expression inhibited human L1.3 retrotransposition to ∼28% of control levels.
source: A3A expression inhibited human L1.3 retrotransposition to ∼28% of control levels (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous reports (Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous reports.

claim: A3A inhibited retrotransposition of TGF21 to ∼20% of control levels.
source: In comparison to control levels, A3A also inhibited retrotransposition of TGF21 (to ∼20%), ZfL2-2 (to ∼17%), and L1SM (to ∼61%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A3A inhibited retrotransposition of ZfL2-2 to ∼17% of control levels.
source: In comparison to control levels, A3A also inhibited retrotransposition of TGF21 (to ∼20%), ZfL2-2 (to ∼17%), and L1SM (to ∼61%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A3A inhibited retrotransposition of L1SM to ∼61% of control levels.
source: In comparison to control levels, A3A also inhibited retrotransposition of TGF21 (to ∼20%), ZfL2-2 (to ∼17%), and L1SM (to ∼61%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The milder inhibition of A3A on L1SM retrotransposition may be due to the GC-rich nature of the L1SM transcript, the elevated steady state levels of L1SM mRNA, and/or an increased number of L1SM retrotransposition events per cell.
source: The milder inhibition of A3A on L1SM retrotransposition may be due to the GC-rich nature of the L1SM transcript, the elevated steady state levels of L1SM mRNA, and/or an increased number of L1SM retrotransposition events per cell (Han and Boeke, 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by a citation to Han and Boeke, 2004.

claim: A deaminase-deficient mutant, A3A-C106S, did not significantly restrict retroelement mobility.
source: A deaminase-deficient mutant, A3A-C106S, did not significantly restrict retroelement mobility (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous studies (Chen et al., 2006; Muckenfuss et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous studies.

claim: A3A inhibited L1.3 retrotransposition when it was expressed from its native 5′UTR on a non-episomal vector.
source: Moreover, A3A inhibited L1.3 retrotransposition when it was expressed from its native 5′UTR on a non-episomal vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D: pKS101/L1.3/sv+).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Human L1s can mobilize by an alternative, endonuclease-independent retrotransposition mechanism (ENi) in cells that lack p53 activity and are defective for components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) DNA repair machinery.
source: In addition to canonical TPRT, human L1s can mobilize by an alternative, endonuclease-independent retrotransposition mechanism (ENi) in cells that lack p53 activity and are defective for components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) DNA repair machinery (Morrish et al., 2002, 2007; Coufal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Morrish et al., 2002, 2007 and Coufal et al., 2011.

claim: A3A expression inhibited WT L1 retrotransposition in both NHEJ-proficient (4364a) and NHEJ-deficient (XR-1) CHO cell lines.
source: A3A expression inhibited WT L1 retrotransposition in both cell lines, and also inhibited ENi retrotransposition in XR-1 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A3A inhibited ENi retrotransposition in XR-1 cells.
source: A3A expression inhibited WT L1 retrotransposition in both cell lines, and also inhibited ENi retrotransposition in XR-1 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A3A can inhibit L1 retrotransposition in a hamster cell line.
source: These data demonstrate A3A can inhibit L1 retrotransposition in a hamster cell line and that the A3A-mediated reduction of L1 retrotransposition is not due to inhibition of L1 EN activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CHO cell assays.

claim: The A3A-mediated reduction of L1 retrotransposition is not due to inhibition of L1 EN activity.
source: These data demonstrate A3A can inhibit L1 retrotransposition in a hamster cell line and that the A3A-mediated reduction of L1 retrotransposition is not due to inhibition of L1 EN activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing A3A inhibits both EN-dependent and EN-independent retrotransposition.

claim: Recombinant A3A (rA3A) has cytidine deaminase activity on single-strand DNA.
source: As expected rA3A had cytidine deaminase activity on single-strand (Figure 2B), but not on double-stranded DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), whereas rA3A_C106S lacked appreciable deaminase activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recombinant A3A (rA3A) does not have cytidine deaminase activity on double-stranded DNA.
source: As expected rA3A had cytidine deaminase activity on single-strand (Figure 2B), but not on double-stranded DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), whereas rA3A_C106S lacked appreciable deaminase activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Recombinant A3A_C106S lacks appreciable deaminase activity.
source: As expected rA3A had cytidine deaminase activity on single-strand (Figure 2B), but not on double-stranded DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), whereas rA3A_C106S lacked appreciable deaminase activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Incorporating increasing amounts of rA3A or rA3A_C106S into LEAP or Moloney murine leukemia virus (MMLV) RT reactions did not significantly affect the synthesis of L1 or MMLV-derived cDNA products.
source: Incorporating increasing amounts of rA3A or rA3A_C106S into LEAP or Moloney murine leukemia virus (MMLV) RT reactions did not significantly affect the synthesis of L1 or MMLV-derived cDNA products (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A3A does not specifically block L1 RT activity.
source: Thus, A3A does not specifically block L1 RT activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no effect on cDNA synthesis.

claim: LEAP products generated in the presence of rA3A contained abundant C-to-U editing that was most frequent at the single 5′-TCA-3′ consensus A3A deamination site present in the single-strand oligonucleotide adapter.
source: In contrast, LEAP products generated in the presence of rA3A contained abundant C-to-U editing that was most frequent at the single 5′-TCA-3′ consensus A3A deamination site (Chen et al., 2006) present in the single-strand oligonucleotide adapter used to prime L1 RT reactions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, top chart in the middle panel, 91 of 100 (91%) total 5′-TCA-3′ sites within the 100 single-strand oligonucleotide adapters showed evidence of deamination).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with citation to Chen et al., 2006 for the consensus site.

claim: 91 of 100 (91%) total 5′-TCA-3′ sites within the 100 single-strand oligonucleotide adapters showed evidence of deamination in LEAP reactions with rA3A.
source: In contrast, LEAP products generated in the presence of rA3A contained abundant C-to-U editing that was most frequent at the single 5′-TCA-3′ consensus A3A deamination site (Chen et al., 2006) present in the single-strand oligonucleotide adapter used to prime L1 RT reactions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, top chart in the middle panel, 91 of 100 (91%) total 5′-TCA-3′ sites within the 100 single-strand oligonucleotide adapters showed evidence of deamination).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only 25 of 600 (4.2%) 5′-TCA-3′ sites within the 100 L1 cDNA products showed evidence of deamination in LEAP reactions with rA3A without RNase H.
source: However, far less deamination was detected within L1 cDNA LEAP products at the six internal 5′-TCA-3′ sites (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, top chart in the middle panel, only 25 of 600 (4.2%) 5′-TCA-3′ sites within the 100 L1 cDNA products showed evidence of deamination).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The L1 cDNA may remain annealed to L1 mRNA, generating L1 mRNA/cDNA heteroduplexes after reverse transcription, thereby leaving only the single-strand oligonucleotide LEAP adapter susceptible to deamination.
source: The non-uniform pattern of deamination events observed above suggested that the L1 cDNA may remain annealed to L1 mRNA, generating L1 mRNA/cDNA heteroduplexes after reverse transcription, thereby leaving only the single-strand oligonucleotide LEAP adapter susceptible to deamination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the non-uniform pattern of deamination events observed in the experiments.

claim: In the presence of rA3A and RNase H, 228 of 600 (38%) 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within the L1 cDNAs showed evidence of deamination.
source: In the presence of rA3A and RNase H, 228 of 600 (38%) 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within the L1 cDNAs showed evidence of deamination (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, bottom chart in the middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of rA3A_C106S and RNase H, only 6.7% of 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within 100 L1 cDNAs demonstrated evidence of deamination.
source: In contrast, in the presence of rA3A_C106S and RNase H, only 6.7% of 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within 100 L1 cDNAs demonstrated evidence of deamination (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, bottom chart in the right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In reactions conducted with RNase H alone, 4.2% of 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within 100 L1 cDNAs contained signatures of deamination.
source: Similarly, in reactions conducted with RNase H alone, 4.2% of 5′-TCA-3′ substrates within 100 L1 cDNAs contained signatures of deamination (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, bottom chart in the left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The slightly increased number of deamination events observed with RNase H alone may reflect endogenous cytidine deaminase activity present in HeLa RNP preparations.
source: The slightly increased number of deamination events observed with RNase H alone may reflect endogenous cytidine deaminase activity present in HeLa RNP preparations.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observed data.

claim: APOBEC3B (A3B) might be responsible for endogenous deamination events as it is expressed in HeLa cells and can suppress L1 retrotransposition.
source: APOBEC3B (A3B) might be responsible for these events as it is expressed in HeLa cells and can suppress L1 retrotransposition (Chen et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Wissing et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Bogerd et al., 2006b; Wissing et al., 2011.

claim: The L1 cDNA, when annealed to the L1 mRNA in an mRNA/cDNA heteroduplex, is protected from mutation by cellular deaminases.
source: These results suggest that the L1 cDNA, when annealed to the L1 mRNA in an mRNA/cDNA heteroduplex, is protected from mutation by cellular deaminases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing differential deamination with and without RNase H treatment.

claim: Uridine residues are efficiently removed from DNA through combined actions of uracil DNA glycosylase (UNG) and apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease (APE).
source: Uridine residues are efficiently removed from DNA through combined actions of uracil DNA glycosylase (UNG) and apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease (APE) (Krokan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krokan et al., 2002.

claim: UGI expression from a transfected plasmid alleviated A3A-mediated L1 inhibition by ∼twofold (from ∼25% to ∼57% of control levels).
source: Remarkably, UGI expression from a transfected plasmid (pLGCX_UGI) alleviated A3A-mediated L1 inhibition by ∼twofold (Figure 3B: from ∼25% to ∼57% of control levels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: UGI expression had little effect on L1 retrotransposition activity in assays conducted in the presence of A3A deaminase mutant (A3A-C106S) or β-arrestin control.
source: In contrast, UGI expression had little effect on L1 retrotransposition activity in assays conducted in the presence of A3A deaminase mutant (A3A-C106S) or β-arrestin control (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: UGI expression did not affect the ability of deaminase-deficient A3B mutants to inhibit L1 retrotransposition.
source: Similarly, UGI expression did not affect the ability of deaminase-deficient A3B mutants (Bogerd et al., 2006b) to inhibit L1 retrotransposition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A: see A3B_N-term and A3B_CS data).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Bogerd et al., 2006b.

claim: UGI expression specifically alleviates a deaminase-dependent mechanism of L1 retrotransposition inhibition.
source: Thus, UGI expression specifically alleviates a deaminase-dependent mechanism of L1 retrotransposition inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing UGI effects are specific to wild-type A3A.

claim: Characterization of 12 independent retrotransposition events from HeLa cells co-transfected with A3A, UGI, and pJM140/L1.3/Δ2/k7 revealed four G-to-A mutations on the L1 coding strand, which correspond to C-to-U deamination events on the (−) strand L1 cDNA.
source: Characterization of 12 independent retrotransposition events revealed four G-to-A mutations on the L1 coding strand, which correspond to C-to-U deamination events on the (−) strand L1 cDNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 5′ target-site duplication (TSD) of one insertion contained a C-to-T change within a 5′-TCA-3′ consensus A3A deamination site in flanking genomic DNA, leading to an inexact TSD flanking a newly retrotransposed L1.
source: Notably, the 5′ target-site duplication (TSD) of one insertion contained a C-to-T change within a 5′-TCA-3′ consensus A3A deamination site in flanking genomic DNA. This putative A3A-mediated deamination event led to an inexact TSD flanking a newly retrotransposed L1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In control U2OS cells, transfection of a low amount of A3A plasmid (25 ng) inhibited retrotransposition to ∼28.0% of control levels without substantial cytotoxicity.
source: In control U2OS cells, transfection of a low amount of A3A plasmid (25 ng) inhibited retrotransposition to ∼28.0% of control levels without substantial cytotoxicity (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In U2OS_UGI-expressing cells, A3A only slightly inhibited L1 retrotransposition (to ∼83% of control levels).
source: By comparison, in U2OS_UGI-expressing cells, A3A only slightly inhibited L1 retrotransposition (Figure 3E: to ∼83% of control levels; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Stable UGI expression relieves A3A-mediated inhibition of L1 retrotransposition in U2OS cells.
source: Thus, consistent with experiments performed in HeLa cells, stable UGI expression relieves A3A-mediated inhibition of L1 retrotransposition in U2OS cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from U2OS cell assays.

claim: Characterization of 24 control L1 retrotransposition events from U2OS_UGI cells did not reveal any G-to-A mutations.
source: Characterization of 24 control L1 retrotransposition events did not reveal any G-to-A mutations (Figure 3F, top panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Characterization of 30 L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of A3A-C106S revealed only five G-to-A mutations.
source: Similarly, characterization of 30 L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of A3A-C106S revealed only five G-to-A mutations (Figure 3F, middle panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Characterization of 33 L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of A3A revealed 39 G-to-A mutations.
source: In contrast, characterization of 33 L1 retrotransposition events generated in the presence of A3A revealed 39 G-to-A mutations (Figure 3F, bottom panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The A3A-induced mutations occurred in a strand-specific manner (i.e., we only detected one C-to-T mutation on the L1 coding strand).
source: The A3A-induced mutations occurred in a strand-specific manner (i.e., we only detected one C-to-T mutation on the L1 coding strand), and far outnumbered any other nucleotide changes in retrotransposed products.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sequencing of retrotransposition events.

claim: A3A-induced mutations far outnumbered any other nucleotide changes in retrotransposed products.
source: The A3A-induced mutations occurred in a strand-specific manner (i.e., we only detected one C-to-T mutation on the L1 coding strand), and far outnumbered any other nucleotide changes in retrotransposed products.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sequencing of retrotransposition events.

claim: One mutation (pJM140/L1.3/Δ2/k7: G-5390-A) introduced a premature termination codon into L1 ORF2, which would create a 145 amino acid truncation in ORF2p.
source: Notably, one mutation (pJM140/L1.3/Δ2/k7: G-5390-A) introduced a premature termination codon into L1 ORF2, which would create a 145 amino acid truncation in ORF2p.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sequencing analysis.

claim: The G-5390-A mutation reduced L1 retrotransposition efficiency to ∼10% of control levels.
source: This mutation reduced L1 retrotransposition efficiency to ∼10% of control levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The detected A3A-mediated deamination events occur on single-strand DNA during TPRT rather than on L1 mRNA or single-strand episomal plasmid DNA prior to L1 retrotransposition.
source: Thus, coupled with identification of a deamination-induced mutation in genomic DNA flanking a newly retrotransposed L1 (Figure 3D), these data suggest that the detected A3A-mediated deamination events occur on single-strand DNA during TPRT rather than on L1 mRNA or single-strand episomal plasmid DNA prior to L1 retrotransposition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing deamination in flanking genomic DNA.

claim: In the presence of cellular RNase H, the (−) strand L1 cDNA becomes vulnerable to A3A deamination.
source: In the presence of cellular RNase H, the (−) strand L1 cDNA becomes vulnerable to A3A deamination (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Normally, A3A-mediated deamination events would be repaired by combined actions of UNG and APE, which could lead to the integration of a 5′ truncated L1 cDNA that lacks evidence of deamination.
source: Normally, these events would be repaired by combined actions of UNG and APE, which we speculate could lead to the integration of a 5′ truncated L1 cDNA that lacks evidence of deamination.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on known DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: In the presence of ectopically expressed UGI, A3A-mediated deamination events become unveiled in the retrotransposed L1s.
source: However, in the presence of ectopically expressed UGI, A3A-mediated deamination events become unveiled in the retrotransposed L1s (Figure 3D,F, 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D, 3F, and 4A.

claim: A3A can act on transiently exposed single-strand genomic DNA flanking L1 integration sites.
